items.followUp: Explain how transpiration helps in the upward movement of water in plants.

rubric.why: Connects water loss from leaves to the transpiration pull and explains that it moves water upward through the xylem from roots to leaves.
rubric.description: Water evaporates from leaves, mainly through the stomata, creating transpiration pull that draws water upward through the xylem from roots to leaves.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete link from evaporation/transpiration to upward water movement through xylem; award 1 mark if only the pull or the route is correctly described.

rubric.why: Explains how water molecules remain joined as an unbroken column.
rubric.description: Cohesion between water molecules maintains a continuous column of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking cohesion between water molecules with a continuous water column.

rubric.why: Explains how the water column is supported along the xylem.
rubric.description: Adhesion between water molecules and xylem walls helps support the water column.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing adhesion between water and the xylem walls.

rubric.why: Identifies that this upward transport does not require direct energy expenditure by the plant.
rubric.description: Water is transported passively, without direct expenditure of energy by the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the process is passive or occurs without energy expenditure.

modelAnswer: Water evaporates from leaf surfaces and exits mainly through the stomata, producing transpiration pull or tension.
This tension pulls water upward through the xylem from the roots towards the leaves.
Cohesion between water molecules keeps them joined in a continuous column.
Adhesion between water molecules and the xylem walls helps support this column.
Thus, water is transported passively, without direct expenditure of energy by the plant.

items.followUp: What is the organ level of organization? Give one example.

rubric.why: Defines a tissue as a group of similar cells that work together for a function.
rubric.description: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together to perform a particular function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a tissue as similar cells performing a function.

rubric.why: Provides an appropriate example of a tissue.
rubric.description: Muscle tissue is one example of a tissue.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example of a tissue.

modelAnswer: The tissue level is a level of organization in which a group of similar cells work together to perform a particular function.

items.followUp: What are quantitative observations? Give two examples.

rubric.why: Distinguishes qualitative observations from numerical measurements.
rubric.description: Qualitative observations describe qualities or features without using numerical measurements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that qualitative observations are descriptive and non-numerical.

rubric.why: Gives a valid example of a quality that can be observed.
rubric.description: Examples include the colour, smell, texture, or shape of an object.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one or more valid examples.

modelAnswer: Qualitative observations describe qualities or features without using numerical measurements.
Examples include the colour, smell, texture, or shape of an object.

rubric.why: Identifies water movement through a semipermeable membrane in the direction opposite to natural osmosis.
rubric.description: Reverse osmosis is the movement of water through a semipermeable membrane in the direction opposite to natural osmosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water, the semipermeable membrane, and the reversed direction.

rubric.why: States the pressure condition and where it is applied to cause reverse osmosis.
rubric.description: Pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied to the concentrated solution to force water through the membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that pressure greater than osmotic pressure is applied to the concentrated solution.

modelAnswer: Reverse osmosis is the movement of water through a semipermeable membrane in the direction opposite to natural osmosis.
It occurs when pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied to the concentrated solution, forcing water through the membrane.
